bernoulli-distribution.name: Bernoulli
bernoulli-distribution.median: $0$ for $p<1/2$; $1$ for $p>1/2$; any value in $[0,1]$ for $p=1/2$
bernoulli-distribution.description: a two-outcome distribution for a single success or failure
bernoulli-distribution.symbols: where p is the probability of success and x records failure or success
bernoulli-distribution.history:
Bernoulli’s posthumously published *Ars Conjectandi* (1713) studied chance in repeated trials. Its binary trial is the setting from which the success-or-failure model takes its name.{{cite:dodge2008}} (p. 37, “Bernoulli, Jakob”)

Modern probability texts use the Bernoulli variable as the elementary unit whose sums give binomial counts. Binary-response models then let its success probability depend on observed predictors.{{cite:siegrist2022_bernoulli_intro}} (§11.1, Basic Theory){{cite:nelder_wedderburn1972}} (§3.3, p. 379)
bernoulli-distribution.sampling: Draw a uniform value $U$ between zero and one, then return $1$ when $U<p$ and $0$ otherwise, where $p$ is the success probability.
bernoulli-distribution.statistical_use: For an observed yes-or-no outcome, the success probability is estimated by the sample proportion across independent trials. A logistic model lets that probability vary with predictors; the Bernoulli likelihood supplies each observation’s contribution.{{cite:nelder_wedderburn1972}} (§3.3, p. 379) It is the observation model behind binary-response regression and the single-trial component of a binomial count.{{cite:siegrist2022_binomial_distribution}} (§11.2, Distribution Functions)
bernoulli-distribution.worked_example:
### A binary check

If a test flags a defect with probability $p=0.2$, then $P(X=1)=0.2$ and $P(X=0)=0.8$. Its mean is $0.2$, while its variance is $0.2(0.8)=0.16$; the mean is a probability, not a fractional observed outcome.{{cite:siegrist2022_bernoulli_intro}} (§11.1, Basic Theory)

key_result.title: Mean and variance of one trial
key_result.statement: For $X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$, $\mathrm E(X)=p$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=p(1-p)$.{{cite:siegrist2022_bernoulli_intro}} (§11.1, Basic Theory)
key_result.meaning: The expected value is the success probability, while the variance is largest near an even chance.
key_result.proof: Since $X$ is either zero or one, $X^2=X$. Thus $\mathrm E(X)=0(1-p)+1p=p$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathrm E(X^2)-\mathrm E(X)^2=p-p^2=p(1-p)$.{{cite:siegrist2022_bernoulli_intro}} (§11.1, Basic Theory)

beta-distribution.name: Beta
beta-distribution.mode: $(\alpha-1)/(\alpha+\beta-2)$ for $\alpha,\beta>1$; boundary mode if a shape is at most $1$, except all $x\in[0,1]$ when $\alpha=\beta=1$
beta-distribution.description: a continuous distribution for a probability between zero and one
beta-distribution.symbols: where α and β are positive shape parameters, Γ is the gamma function, and x is between zero and one
beta-distribution.statistical_use: Its adjustable shapes make it a standard model for uncertain proportions and a conjugate prior for a binomial success probability. In binomial inference, a beta prior updates by adding observed successes and failures to its two shape parameters. The posterior can be summarised by a mean or credible interval, but those summaries need not coincide when the posterior is skewed.{{cite:gelman_bda2013}} (§2.1, pp. 29–31)
beta-distribution.worked_example:
### A probability below one half

For $X\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,3)$, integration of the density gives $P(X<1/2)=11/16=0.6875$. This is a probability about the unknown proportion under the model; it is not the proportion of successes in any one sample.{{cite:siegrist2022_beta}} (§5.17, Basic Theory)

key_result.title: Mean of a beta probability
key_result.statement: For $X\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$, $\mathrm E(X)=\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)$.{{cite:siegrist2022_beta}} (§5.17, Basic Theory)
key_result.meaning: Each shape contributes to the expected share of the total concentration.
key_result.proof: The density normaliser is $B(\alpha,\beta)$. Multiplying its kernel by $x$ makes the integral $B(\alpha+1,\beta)/B(\alpha,\beta)$. The beta-function identity $B(\alpha+1,\beta)=\alpha B(\alpha,\beta)/(\alpha+\beta)$ gives the stated mean.{{cite:siegrist2022_beta}} (§5.17, Basic Theory)

binomial-distribution.name: Binomial
binomial-distribution.mode: $\lfloor(n+1)p\rfloor$; also one less if $(n+1)p\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ is an integer
binomial-distribution.description: a count distribution for successes in a fixed number of independent trials
binomial-distribution.symbols: where n is the number of trials, p is the success probability, and x is the number of successes
binomial-distribution.history:
Bernoulli’s *Ars Conjectandi*, published in 1713, developed combinatorial calculations for repeated trials. Counting the number of successes gives the binomial sampling problem.{{cite:edwards2013_ars}} (§§“Part I” and “Part IV”)

The distribution later became a standard likelihood for a population proportion. Modern inference distinguishes exact binomial calculations from approximations that rely on larger samples.{{cite:dodge2008}} (pp. 44–45, “Binomial Distribution”){{cite:siegrist2022_binomial_distribution}} (§11.2, The Normal Approximation)
binomial-distribution.sampling: Draw $n$ independent Bernoulli values with success probability $p$ and add them, where $n$ is the trial count.
binomial-distribution.statistical_use: A binomial likelihood estimates a common success probability from a fixed number of independent trials. Exact tail probabilities support tests and confidence intervals; if trials are dependent or their probabilities differ, the binomial model needs reconsideration. It supplies exact probabilities for repeated binary trials and underlies inference about a population proportion.{{cite:siegrist2022_binomial_distribution}} (§11.2, Distribution Functions and The Normal Approximation)
binomial-distribution.worked_example:
### Three successes in ten trials

For $n=10$ and $p=0.3$, $P(X=3)=\binom{10}{3}(0.3)^3(0.7)^7\approx0.2668$. The count $3$ is one possible outcome; its probability is not the same as the estimated success rate $3/10$.{{cite:siegrist2022_binomial_distribution}} (§11.2, The Probability Mass Function)

key_result.title: Mean and variance of a trial count
key_result.statement: For $X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)$, $\mathrm E(X)=np$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p)$.{{cite:siegrist2022_binomial_distribution}} (§11.2, Moments)
key_result.meaning: The count grows as a sum of independent binary outcomes, so both its mean and variance scale with the number of trials.
key_result.proof: Write $X=\sum_{i=1}^n B_i$ for independent Bernoulli variables with success probability $p$. Linearity gives $\mathrm E(X)=\sum_i p=np$; independence removes cross-covariances, so $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sum_i p(1-p)=np(1-p)$.{{cite:siegrist2022_binomial_distribution}} (§11.2, Moments)

cauchy-distribution.name: Cauchy
cauchy-distribution.description: a heavy-tailed distribution on the real line whose mean does not exist
cauchy-distribution.symbols: where x₀ is the location, γ is the positive scale, and x is the observed value
cauchy-distribution.sampling: Draw $U$ uniformly between zero and one and set $X=x_0+\gamma\tan[\pi(U-1/2)]$, where $x_0$ is the location and $\gamma$ is the scale.
cauchy-distribution.lead_context: Its extreme tails make it a useful counterexample to methods that require a finite mean or variance.{{cite:casella_berger2002}}
cauchy-distribution.statistical_use: A Cauchy likelihood can model outliers, but a sample average does not become stable as the sample grows. For location inference, the sample median or a likelihood-based fit is more informative than the sample mean under this model.{{cite:casella_berger2002}}
cauchy-distribution.worked_example:
### Half the mass near the centre

For a standard Cauchy variable, $F(1)-F(-1)=(3/4)-(1/4)=1/2$. The interval $[-1,1]$ contains half the probability even though the distribution has no finite mean.{{cite:forbes2011}}

key_result.title: Why the mean does not exist
key_result.statement: A Cauchy variable with positive scale $\gamma$ has no finite absolute first moment, so its usual expectation is undefined.{{cite:forbes2011}}
key_result.meaning: This is why the sample average is not a reliable location summary under the Cauchy model.
key_result.proof: For sufficiently large $|x|$, the density $\gamma/[\pi((x-x_0)^2+\gamma^2)]$ is bounded below by a positive constant times $1/x^2$. The tail integral of $|x|f(x)$ therefore dominates a constant times $\int_M^\infty dx/x$, which diverges. Hence $\mathrm E|X|=\infty$ and the ordinary expectation is not defined.{{cite:forbes2011}}

chi-squared-distribution.name: Chi-squared
chi-squared-distribution.description: a distribution for sums of squares of independent standard normal variables
chi-squared-distribution.symbols: where ν is the degrees of freedom, Γ is the gamma function, and x is positive
chi-squared-distribution.history:
Pearson’s 1900 paper studied the discrepancy between observed and expected frequencies under a probability model. That problem led to the chi-squared goodness-of-fit statistic and its reference distribution.{{cite:pearson1900}}

The same distribution also arises exactly as a sum of squared standard normal variables. Modern texts separate that exact normal-sampling result from the asymptotic chi-squared calibration of many fit statistics.{{cite:casella_berger2002}}
chi-squared-distribution.sampling:
For a positive integer $
u$, draw $
u$ independent standard normal values and add their squares, where $
u$ is the degrees of freedom.
chi-squared-distribution.lead_context: It calibrates sample-variance inference under normal sampling and appears in large-sample goodness-of-fit tests, where fitted parameters change the reference degrees of freedom.{{cite:siegrist2022_normals}} (§6.08) {{cite:fisher1922_chisq}} (pp. 87–90)
chi-squared-distribution.statistical_use: For independent normal observations, a scaled sample variance has a chi-squared law and gives exact variance intervals. Pearson-type goodness-of-fit statistics use a chi-squared reference asymptotically, with degrees of freedom adjusted for fitted parameters.{{cite:casella_berger2002}}
chi-squared-distribution.worked_example:
### Four squared normal components

If $X$ is the sum of squares of four independent standard normal variables, then $X\sim\chi^2_4$. Its mean is $4$ and its variance is $8$, so a value near $4$ is typical but the distribution is not symmetric.{{cite:forbes2011}}

key_result.title: Mean and variance of squared normals
key_result.statement:
If $X\sim\chi^2_
u$ with integer $
u\ge1$, then $\mathrm E(X)=
u$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=2
u$.{{cite:casella_berger2002}}
key_result.meaning: Each squared standard-normal component adds one to the mean and two to the variance.

conway-maxwell-poisson-distribution.name: Conway–Maxwell–Poisson
conway-maxwell-poisson-distribution.description: a flexible count distribution that can model underdispersion or overdispersion
conway-maxwell-poisson-distribution.symbols: where λ is the rate parameter, ν controls dispersion, Z is the normalising constant, and x is a count
conway-maxwell-poisson-distribution.history:
Conway and Maxwell introduced this count model in 1962 while studying queues with state-dependent service rates. The factorial-power parameter changed how concentrated the queue-length counts could be.{{cite:conway_maxwell1962}}

Shmueli and colleagues revived the family in 2005 for fitting dispersed discrete data. Later mean-parameterised regression work made its coefficients easier to compare with other count models.{{cite:shmueli2005}}{{cite:huang2017_cmp}}
conway-maxwell-poisson-distribution.lead_context: It is used when count data are either more or less dispersed than a Poisson model allows.{{cite:shmueli2005}}
conway-maxwell-poisson-distribution.statistical_use: In count regression, this family can accommodate both overdispersion and underdispersion. Its original $\lambda$ parameter is generally not the mean, so a fitted coefficient needs a mean-parameterised formulation or a careful translation before comparison with Poisson regression.{{cite:huang2017_cmp}}
conway-maxwell-poisson-distribution.worked_example:
### A normalising constant that can be summed

At $\nu=0$ and $\lambda=1/2$, the normalising series is $Z=\sum_{x=0}^{\infty}(1/2)^x=2$. Thus $P(X=0)=1/2$, $P(X=1)=1/4$, and $P(X\le1)=3/4$. This endpoint is a geometric count on nonnegative integers, not the trial-count convention used on the geometric article.{{cite:shmueli2005}}
conway-maxwell-poisson-distribution.definition_note: Here $Z(\lambda,\nu)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\lambda^j/(j!)^\nu$; the stated parameter restrictions make this normalising sum finite.{{cite:shmueli2005}}

key_result.title: The Poisson special case
key_result.statement: At $\nu=1$, the Conway–Maxwell–Poisson law with parameter $\lambda$ is $\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)$.{{cite:shmueli2005}}
key_result.meaning: The extra dispersion parameter changes the count law away from this Poisson baseline.
key_result.proof: At $\nu=1$, the normalising series becomes $Z(\lambda,1)=\sum_{j=0}^\infty\lambda^j/j!=e^\lambda$. The mass is therefore $\lambda^x/(x!e^\lambda)=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x/x!$, exactly the Poisson mass.{{cite:shmueli2005}}

dirichlet-distribution.name: Dirichlet
dirichlet-distribution.description: a multivariate distribution for a vector of category probabilities
dirichlet-distribution.symbols: where α is the vector of positive concentration parameters and x is a vector of category probabilities
dirichlet-distribution.conjugate_prior_for: $\boldsymbol X\mid\boldsymbol p\sim\operatorname{Mult}(n,\boldsymbol p)$, giving $\boldsymbol p\mid\boldsymbol x\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\boldsymbol\alpha+\boldsymbol x)$
dirichlet-distribution.lead_context: It models uncertain category-probability vectors and updates directly with multinomial counts.{{cite:gelman_bda2013}}
dirichlet-distribution.statistical_use: A Dirichlet prior adds observed counts componentwise to its concentration vector in a multinomial analysis. The posterior means combine prior category weights with observed frequencies, while the common total means the components are dependent.{{cite:gelman_bda2013}}
dirichlet-distribution.worked_example:
### Updating three categories

Start with $\boldsymbol p\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(2,3,5)$ and observe counts $(4,1,0)$. The posterior is $\operatorname{Dirichlet}(6,4,5)$, so the posterior mean of $p_1$ is $6/15=0.4$, compared with prior mean $2/10=0.2$.{{cite:gelman_bda2013}}
dirichlet-distribution.definition_note: The vector $\boldsymbol\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_K)$ has $K$ positive components, $\alpha_0=\sum_k\alpha_k$, and an observed vector $\boldsymbol x=(x_1,\ldots,x_K)$ lies on the simplex: each $x_k>0$ and $\sum_kx_k=1$.{{cite:forbes2011}}

key_result.title: Beta marginal of one component
key_result.statement: If $\boldsymbol X\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_K)$ and $\alpha_0=\sum_k\alpha_k$, then $X_j\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha_j,\alpha_0-\alpha_j)$ for $K\ge2$.{{cite:gelman_bda2013}}
key_result.meaning: Each category probability has a beta marginal even though the category probabilities are dependent.
key_result.proof: Let independent $G_k\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha_k,1)$ and set $X_k=G_k/\sum_iG_i$. The sum $S_{-j}=\sum_{i\ne j}G_i$ is independent of $G_j$ and has gamma shape $\alpha_0-\alpha_j$ with the same rate. The ratio $G_j/(G_j+S_{-j})$ is beta with the stated shapes.{{cite:gelman_bda2013}}

exponential-distribution.name: Exponential
exponential-distribution.description: a continuous distribution for the waiting time to the next event in a Poisson process
exponential-distribution.symbols: where λ is the positive event rate and x is a waiting time
exponential-distribution.sampling: Draw $U$ uniformly between zero and one and set $X=-\log U/\lambda$, where $\lambda$ is the event rate.
exponential-distribution.statistical_use: Its constant event rate makes it the basic waiting-time model for Poisson processes and reliability calculations. An exponential likelihood estimates a constant event rate from observed waiting times, with total exposure carrying the information about the rate. The constant-hazard assumption should be checked when failure risk changes with age.{{cite:nist_exponential_reliability}} (§8.1.6.1, failure and reliability functions)
exponential-distribution.worked_example:
### Waiting longer than five units

At rate $\lambda=0.2$ per unit, $P(X>5)=e^{-0.2(5)}=e^{-1}\approx0.3679$. Conditional on surviving five units, the chance of surviving another five is the same $e^{-1}$ by memorylessness.{{cite:siegrist2022_exponential}} (§14.2, Memoryless Property)

key_result.title: Memorylessness
key_result.statement: For $X\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)$ and $s,t\ge0$, $P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t)=e^{-\lambda t}$.{{cite:siegrist2022_exponential}} (§14.2, Memoryless Property)
key_result.meaning: Elapsed waiting time does not change the distribution of the remaining wait.
key_result.proof: The survival function is $S(u)=e^{-\lambda u}$, which is positive for every finite $u$. Hence $P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=S(s+t)/S(s)=e^{-\lambda(s+t)}/e^{-\lambda s}=e^{-\lambda t}=S(t)$.{{cite:siegrist2022_exponential}} (§14.2, Memoryless Property)

f-distribution.name: F
f-distribution.description: a distribution for ratios of independent scaled chi-squared variables
f-distribution.symbols: where d₁ and d₂ are numerator and denominator degrees of freedom, B is the beta function, and x is positive
f-distribution.lead_context: It supplies reference distributions for ratios of variance estimates and for analysis-of-variance tests.{{cite:casella_berger2002}}
f-distribution.statistical_use: Under normal-model assumptions, a ratio of independent scaled sums of squares has an F reference law. This calibrates variance comparisons and nested-model tests; the two degrees of freedom identify the numerator and denominator sources separately.{{cite:casella_berger2002}}
f-distribution.worked_example:
### A finite mean

For $X\sim F_{5,10}$, the mean exists because the denominator degrees of freedom exceed two, and equals $10/(10-2)=1.25$. It is above one even though the ratio is centred near one in many null-model applications.{{cite:forbes2011}}

key_result.title: When the mean of an F ratio exists
key_result.statement: If $X\sim F_{d_1,d_2}$ and $d_2>2$, then $\mathrm E(X)=d_2/(d_2-2)$.{{cite:forbes2011}}
key_result.meaning: The denominator degrees of freedom control whether the ratio has a finite mean.
key_result.proof: Write $X=(U/d_1)/(V/d_2)$ with independent $U\sim\chi^2_{d_1}$ and $V\sim\chi^2_{d_2}$. Then $\mathrm E(U)=d_1$ and the gamma integral gives $\mathrm E(1/V)=1/(d_2-2)$ when $d_2>2$. Independence yields $\mathrm E(X)=(d_2/d_1)d_1/(d_2-2)$.{{cite:forbes2011}}

gamma-distribution.name: Gamma
gamma-distribution.description: a continuous distribution for positive quantities such as waiting times
gamma-distribution.symbols: where α is the shape, λ is the rate, Γ is the gamma function, and x is positive
gamma-distribution.statistical_use: A gamma model can describe positive durations or responses whose variability grows with their mean. In Bayesian count models, a gamma prior for a Poisson intensity yields a gamma posterior after adding event counts and exposure.{{cite:gelman_bda2013}} (§2.7, pp. 47–50, Poisson–Gamma update)
gamma-distribution.worked_example:
### Two arrivals in a Poisson process

For $X\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(2,1/2)$ in shape-rate form, the mean is $2/(1/2)=4$. Its survival beyond time $4$ is $e^{-2}(1+2)\approx0.4060$, the probability that fewer than two events have occurred by that time in a rate-$1/2$ Poisson process.{{cite:siegrist2022_gamma_waiting}} (§14.3, arrival times)
gamma-distribution.definition_note: This article uses $\lambda$ for the gamma rate. Examples using $\beta$ or $b$ for the rate describe the same shape–rate law; a scale parameter is the reciprocal of rate.{{cite:nist_gamma_handbook}} (§8.1.6.5, rate and scale conventions)

key_result.title: Mean and variance in shape-rate form
key_result.statement: For $X\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha,\lambda)$, $\mathrm E(X)=\alpha/\lambda$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\alpha/\lambda^2$.{{cite:nist_gamma_handbook}} (§8.1.6.5, mean and variance)
key_result.meaning: Increasing the shape raises the mean, while increasing the rate shortens the waiting-time scale.
key_result.proof: Write $f(x)=\lambda^\alpha x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\lambda x}/\Gamma(\alpha)$ for $x>0$. The substitution $u=\lambda x$ gives $\int_0^\infty f(x)\,dx=1$ and $F(x)=\gamma(\alpha,\lambda x)/\Gamma(\alpha)$. More generally, the gamma integral gives $\mathbb E(X^r)=\Gamma(\alpha+r)/[\Gamma(\alpha)\lambda^r]$ for $r>-\alpha$. At $r=1,2$ this yields $\mathbb E X=\alpha/\lambda$ and $\operatorname{Var}X=\alpha/\lambda^2$. The same integral gives $M(t)=(1-t/\lambda)^{-\alpha}$ for $t<\lambda$ and characteristic function $M(it)$. Expanding $\log M(t)=-\alpha\log(1-t/\lambda)$ gives cumulants $\kappa_r=\alpha(r-1)!/\lambda^r$; hence skewness $2/\sqrt\alpha$ and excess kurtosis $6/\alpha$. Multiplication of MGFs proves that independent gamma variables with a common rate add their shapes. The derivative of $\log f(x)$ with respect to $x$ is $(\alpha-1)/x-\lambda$, giving interior mode $(\alpha-1)/\lambda$ for $\alpha>1$ and a boundary mode at zero otherwise. Differentiating the normalizing identity with respect to $\alpha$ gives $\mathbb E\log X=\psi(\alpha)-\log\lambda$. Substitution into $-\mathbb E\log f(X)$ gives the displayed entropy. Finally the expected negative Hessian of $\log f$ in $(\alpha,\lambda)$ has entries $\psi_1(\alpha)$, $-1/\lambda$, and $\alpha/\lambda^2$, proving the Fisher-information matrix. For a Poisson likelihood $\theta^S e^{-n\theta}$, multiplying by the gamma prior kernel $\theta^{\alpha-1}e^{-\lambda\theta}$ gives the gamma posterior with shape $\alpha+S$ and rate $\lambda+n$.{{cite:siegrist2022_gamma}} (§5.8, density, moments, MGF and relations){{cite:nist_gamma_handbook}} (§8.1.6.5, gamma moments){{cite:gelman_bda2013}} (§2.7, pp. 47–50, Poisson–Gamma update)

geometric-distribution.name: Geometric
geometric-distribution.description: a count distribution for the number of trials until the first success
geometric-distribution.symbols: where p is the probability of success and x is the trial on which the first success occurs
geometric-distribution.lead_context: It models how many independent trials are needed for a first success and gives a discrete memoryless waiting time.{{cite:ross2019}}
geometric-distribution.statistical_use: The geometric likelihood applies when each attempt has the same success probability and trials are independent. The trial-count convention used here starts at one; software that counts failures before success reports a value one smaller.{{cite:ross2019}}
geometric-distribution.worked_example:
### Waiting for a successful attempt

With success probability $p=1/4$, the chance that the first three attempts fail is $P(X>3)=(3/4)^3=27/64\approx0.4219$. The expected trial of the first success is $1/p=4$.{{cite:ross2019}}

key_result.title: Survival and expected trial count
key_result.statement: For a geometric trial count $X$ with success probability $p>0$, $P(X>m)=(1-p)^m$ for integers $m\ge0$, and $\mathrm E(X)=1/p$.{{cite:ross2019}}
key_result.meaning: The survival formula is the chance of repeated failures; it also makes the mean waiting time easy to compute.
key_result.proof: The event $X>m$ says that the first $m$ independent trials all failed, giving $(1-p)^m$. For a positive-integer count, $\mathrm E(X)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty P(X>m)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty(1-p)^m=1/p$.{{cite:ross2019}}

hypergeometric-distribution.name: Hypergeometric
hypergeometric-distribution.description: a count distribution for successes in draws without replacement
hypergeometric-distribution.symbols: where N is the population size, r is the number of successes in it, n is the sample size, and x is the number drawn
hypergeometric-distribution.lead_context: It gives exact sampling probabilities when draws are made without replacement from a finite population.{{cite:feller1968}}
hypergeometric-distribution.statistical_use: The hypergeometric law is appropriate for a fixed-size random sample from a finite set with a known number of marked items. It supplies the conditional calculation behind Fisher’s exact test and shows the finite-population correction absent from a binomial model.{{cite:agresti2002}}
hypergeometric-distribution.worked_example:
### No marked items in a sample

A population has $N=20$ items, of which $r=5$ are marked. For a sample of $n=4$ without replacement, $P(X=0)=\binom{15}{4}/\binom{20}{4}=1365/4845\approx0.2817$.{{cite:feller1968}}

key_result.title: Finite-population mean and variance
key_result.statement: For $X\sim\operatorname{Hypergeom}(N,r,n)$ with $N>1$ and $p=r/N$, $\mathrm E(X)=np$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p)(N-n)/(N-1)$.{{cite:feller1968}}
key_result.meaning: Sampling without replacement keeps the binomial mean but reduces variance by the finite-population factor.
key_result.proof: Let $I_i$ indicate a marked item on draw $i$. Every draw has $\mathrm E(I_i)=p$ and variance $p(1-p)$. For distinct draws, $P(I_i=I_j=1)=r(r-1)/[N(N-1)]$, giving $\operatorname{Cov}(I_i,I_j)=-p(1-p)/(N-1)$. Summing the $n$ indicator means and their $n(n-1)$ ordered cross-covariances gives the stated formulas.{{cite:feller1968}}

inverse-gamma-distribution.name: Inverse gamma
inverse-gamma-distribution.description: a continuous distribution for positive scales and variances
inverse-gamma-distribution.symbols: where α is the shape, β is the scale, Γ is the gamma function, and x is positive
inverse-gamma-distribution.mode_explanation: The mode is $\beta/(\alpha+1)$, which is not the variance.
inverse-gamma-distribution.lead_context: Its reciprocal-gamma construction makes it a traditional prior model for a normal variance.{{cite:raiffa_schlaifer1961}} (Ch. 11, §11.1.3, pp. 290–291)
inverse-gamma-distribution.statistical_use: For a normal likelihood with known mean, an inverse-gamma prior on the variance updates by adding half the sample size to its shape and half the squared-deviation sum to its scale. This convenience does not by itself make a particular prior weakly informative.{{cite:raiffa_schlaifer1961}} (Ch. 11, §11.1.3, pp. 290–291) {{cite:gelman2006}} (§§4.3, 5.1, pp. 522–524)
inverse-gamma-distribution.worked_example:
### Mean and mode differ

For $X\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(3,2)$, the mean is $2/(3-1)=1$, the mode is $2/(3+1)=1/2$, and the variance is $2^2/[(3-1)^2(3-2)]=1$. The equality of this example’s mean and variance is accidental.{{cite:stan_functions2026}} (§“Inverse gamma Distribution”)

key_result.title: The inverse-gamma mode
key_result.statement: For $X\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha,\beta)$ with positive shape and scale, the mode is $\beta/(\alpha+1)$.{{cite:stan_functions2026}} (§“Inverse gamma Distribution”)
key_result.meaning: The most likely density location is below the mean whenever the mean exists.
key_result.proof: Apart from a constant, $\log f(x)=-(\alpha+1)\log x-\beta/x$ for $x>0$. Its derivative is $[\beta-(\alpha+1)x]/x^2$, positive below $\beta/(\alpha+1)$ and negative above it. Thus that stationary point is the global mode.{{cite:stan_functions2026}} (§“Inverse gamma Distribution”)

inverse-gaussian-distribution.name: Inverse Gaussian
inverse-gaussian-distribution.description: a continuous distribution for positive, right-skewed measurements
inverse-gaussian-distribution.symbols: where μ is the mean, λ is the shape, and x is a positive value
inverse-gaussian-distribution.lead_context: Its variance grows rapidly with the mean, which makes it useful for skewed positive responses in generalised linear models.{{cite:mccullagh_nelder1989}}
inverse-gaussian-distribution.statistical_use: An inverse-Gaussian response model is used for positive outcomes with a variance proportional to the cube of the mean at fixed shape. A log link can keep fitted means positive even though the family’s canonical link is inverse quadratic.{{cite:mccullagh_nelder1989}}
inverse-gaussian-distribution.worked_example:
### A skewed positive response

For $X\sim\operatorname{IG}(2,4)$, the mean is $\mu=2$ and the variance is $\mu^3/\lambda=8/4=2$. Doubling the mean while keeping shape $\lambda=4$ would multiply the variance by eight.{{cite:forbes2011}}

key_result.title: Mean and variance of the positive law
key_result.statement: For $X\sim\operatorname{IG}(\mu,\lambda)$, $\mathrm E(X)=\mu$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mu^3/\lambda$.{{cite:forbes2011}}
key_result.meaning: At fixed shape, variability increases cubically with the mean.
key_result.proof: The moment-generating function is $M(t)=\exp\{(\lambda/\mu)[1-\sqrt{1-2\mu^2t/\lambda}]\}$ near zero. Expanding its logarithm gives $\log M(t)=\mu t+(\mu^3/2\lambda)t^2+O(t^3)$. The first two cumulants are therefore $\mu$ and $\mu^3/\lambda$.{{cite:forbes2011}}

lognormal-distribution.name: Lognormal
lognormal-distribution.description: a positive distribution obtained by exponentiating a normal random variable
lognormal-distribution.symbols: where μ and σ are the mean and standard deviation of the underlying normal variable and x is positive

notation_symbols.meaning: standard deviation on the log scale

lognormal-distribution.lead_context: It describes positive measurements built from multiplicative changes and is analysed conveniently on a logarithmic scale.{{cite:forbes2011}}
lognormal-distribution.statistical_use: A lognormal model can be fitted by analysing the logarithms with normal-model tools, then transforming predictions back carefully. The arithmetic mean on the original scale exceeds the median, so exponentiating a fitted log mean gives the median rather than the mean.{{cite:forbes2011}}
lognormal-distribution.worked_example:
### A threshold on the original scale

If $\log X\sim N(0,1)$, then $P(X>e)=P(Z>1)\approx0.1587$ for a standard normal $Z$. The median of $X$ is $1$ while its mean is $e^{1/2}\approx1.6487$.{{cite:forbes2011}}

key_result.title: Moments from a normal logarithm
key_result.statement: If $\log X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, then $\mathrm E(X)=e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=(e^{\sigma^2}-1)e^{2\mu+\sigma^2}$.{{cite:forbes2011}}
key_result.meaning: The arithmetic mean exceeds the median because the upper tail contributes strongly to the average.
key_result.proof: For $Y=\log X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, the normal moment-generating formula gives $\mathrm E(X^k)=\mathrm E(e^{kY})=e^{k\mu+k^2\sigma^2/2}$. Take $k=1,2$ and subtract $[\mathrm E(X)]^2$ from $\mathrm E(X^2)$ to obtain the variance.{{cite:forbes2011}}

multinomial-distribution.name: Multinomial
multinomial-distribution.description: a distribution for counts across several categories in a fixed number of trials
multinomial-distribution.symbols: where n is the number of trials, p is the vector of category probabilities, and x is the vector of counts
multinomial-distribution.lead_context: It is the joint count model for categorical trials and supplies likelihoods for category probabilities.{{cite:agresti2002}}
multinomial-distribution.statistical_use: The multinomial likelihood estimates a vector of category probabilities from counts that sum to a fixed total. Marginal counts are binomial, but their dependence matters in joint intervals and tests of category patterns.{{cite:agresti2002}}
multinomial-distribution.worked_example:
### Counts in three categories

For $n=10$ and $\boldsymbol p=(0.2,0.3,0.5)$, the count vector $(2,3,5)$ has probability $10!/(2!3!5!)\,(0.2)^2(0.3)^3(0.5)^5=0.08505$. The three counts must sum to ten.{{cite:forbes2011}}
multinomial-distribution.definition_note: There are $K$ categories; $\boldsymbol p=(p_1,\ldots,p_K)$ has nonnegative components summing to one, and the realised count vector $\boldsymbol x=(x_1,\ldots,x_K)$ has nonnegative integer components summing to $n$.{{cite:forbes2011}}

key_result.title: Binomial marginals and dependent counts
key_result.statement: For $\boldsymbol X\sim\operatorname{Mult}(n,\boldsymbol p)$, each $X_k\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p_k)$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(X_j,X_k)=-np_jp_k$ for $j\ne k$.{{cite:agresti2002}}
key_result.meaning: A category has a binomial count, but different categories compete for the same fixed total.
key_result.proof: Write $X_k=\sum_{i=1}^n I_{ik}$, where $I_{ik}$ indicates category $k$ on trial $i$. The indicators are independent across trials, so each sum is binomial. For $j\ne k$ on one trial, $I_{ij}I_{ik}=0$, hence covariance $-p_jp_k$; cross-trial covariances vanish, giving $-np_jp_k$.{{cite:agresti2002}}

multivariate-normal-distribution.name: Multivariate normal
multivariate-normal-distribution.description: a joint distribution for a vector of normally distributed measurements
multivariate-normal-distribution.symbols: where μ is the mean vector, Σ is the covariance matrix, and x is an observation vector
multivariate-normal-distribution.lead_context: Its mean vector and covariance matrix describe location, spread and dependence for measurements recorded together.{{cite:strimmer2025_mva}} (Ch. 1, §§1.1, 1.3)
multivariate-normal-distribution.statistical_use: Multivariate-normal models describe correlated measurements jointly in mean estimation, prediction and classification. Fitting each coordinate separately discards the cross-covariances needed for joint uncertainty.{{cite:strimmer2025_mva}} (Ch. 1, §§1.1, 1.3)
multivariate-normal-distribution.worked_example:
### A correlated sum

Let $(X_1,X_2)$ have means zero, unit variances and correlation $0.6$. Then $X_1+X_2$ is normal with variance $1+1+2(0.6)=3.2$, and symmetry gives $P(X_1+X_2>0)=1/2$.{{cite:wang2025_foundations}} (Ch. 6 Extra, Thm. 31, Ex. 32)
multivariate-normal-distribution.definition_note: For a $p$-component vector, $\boldsymbol\mu$ is its $p$-component mean, $\Sigma$ is a positive-definite $p\times p$ covariance matrix, and $\boldsymbol x$ is an observed vector; $|\Sigma|$ denotes its determinant.{{cite:strimmer2025_mva}} (Ch. 1, §1.3, “Multivariate normal model”)

key_result.title: Affine images remain jointly normal
key_result.statement: If $\boldsymbol X\sim\operatorname N_p(\boldsymbol\mu,\Sigma)$, $A$ is a fixed $q\times p$ matrix, and $\boldsymbol b$ is a fixed $q$-vector, then $A\boldsymbol X+\boldsymbol b$ is jointly normal with mean $A\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol b$ and covariance $A\Sigma A^\top$.{{cite:wang2025_foundations}} (Ch. 6 Extra, Thm. 31)
key_result.meaning: Linear combinations and marginals can be analysed without leaving the normal family.
key_result.proof: The characteristic function of $\boldsymbol X$ at $\boldsymbol t$ is $\exp(i\boldsymbol t^\top\boldsymbol\mu-\boldsymbol t^\top\Sigma\boldsymbol t/2)$. Substituting $A^\top\boldsymbol t$ and multiplying by $e^{i\boldsymbol t^\top\boldsymbol b}$ yields the characteristic function of a normal vector with the stated mean and covariance, including a possibly singular covariance when $A$ has deficient rank.{{cite:wang2025_foundations}} (Ch. 6 Extra, Thm. 31 and proof)

negative-binomial-distribution.name: Negative binomial
negative-binomial-distribution.description: a count distribution that allows variance greater than its mean
negative-binomial-distribution.symbols: where μ is the mean count, ν is the dispersion parameter, Γ is the gamma function, and x is a count
negative-binomial-distribution.lead_context: It accommodates count variation beyond the mean–variance equality imposed by a Poisson model.{{cite:venables_ripley2002}}
negative-binomial-distribution.statistical_use: Negative-binomial regression is used for overdispersed counts when a Poisson fit understates variation. In this parameterisation $\mu$ is the mean and $\nu$ controls extra variance; larger $\nu$ brings the law closer to Poisson.{{cite:venables_ripley2002}}
negative-binomial-distribution.worked_example:
### Extra variation in counts

For $X\sim\operatorname{NegBin}(\mu=4,\nu=2)$, the variance is $4+4^2/2=12$, three times the mean. The chance of zero counts is $(2/(4+2))^2=1/9$, larger than the Poisson zero chance $e^{-4}$.{{cite:venables_ripley2002}}

key_result.title: Extra variance from rate mixing
key_result.statement: For the mean-dispersion parameterisation $X\sim\operatorname{NegBin}(\mu,\nu)$, $\mathrm E(X)=\mu$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mu+\mu^2/\nu$.{{cite:venables_ripley2002}}
key_result.meaning: The additional term measures variation beyond the Poisson mean–variance equality.
key_result.proof:
Let $\Lambda\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(
u,
u/\mu)$ in shape-rate form and $X\mid\Lambda\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\Lambda)$. Integrating the Poisson mass against the gamma density gives the displayed negative-binomial mass. The laws of total expectation and variance give $\mathrm E(X)=\mathrm E(\Lambda)=\mu$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathrm E(\Lambda)+\operatorname{Var}(\Lambda)=\mu+\mu^2/
u$.{{cite:venables_ripley2002}}

negative-binomial-distribution.definition_note:
This page uses mean $\mu$ and dispersion $
u$. For integer $
u$, a common alternative counts failures before $
u$ successes with success probability $p=
u/(\mu+
u)$; that convention yields the same mass function.{{cite:forbes2011}}

normal-distribution.name: Normal
normal-distribution.conjugate_prior: [Inverse-Gamma distribution](inverse-gamma-distribution.qmd): $\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha,\beta)$ for a normal sample with known $\mu$, giving $\operatorname{InvGamma}(\alpha+n/2,\beta+S_\mu/2)$
normal-distribution.description: a symmetric bell-shaped distribution for measurements on the real line
normal-distribution.symbols: where μ is the mean, σ is the positive standard deviation, and x is an observed value.{{cite:siegrist2022_normal_distribution}} (§5.6, “The General Normal Distribution”)
normal-distribution.history:
Abraham de Moivre derived a normal-shaped approximation to the symmetric binomial distribution in a 1733 pamphlet, decades before the curve became associated with Gauss. Laplace developed the approximation for binomial counts and later showed how normal errors arise for averages of many observations.{{cite:daw1966_normal_history}} (pp. 3–4) {{cite:oliveira2022_probability_history}} (§9, pp. e20220087-15–e20220087-16)

In his 1809 work on the motion of bodies around the Sun, Gauss used a normal error law while estimating an orbit from observations. This was a different route to the same curve: a model for measurement errors in an astronomical calculation.{{cite:oliveira2022_probability_history}} (§11, pp. e20220087-18–e20220087-19)

In 1958 George Box and Mervin Muller published a way to turn two independent uniform random numbers into two independent normal random numbers. Their short note addressed the practical problem of producing normal deviates on a computer.{{cite:box_muller1958}} (pp. 610–611)

A modern account uses the normal distribution both as a model for observations and as an approximation to sampling distributions. The Bayesian normal-mean calculation in Gelman and colleagues’ 2013 text illustrates how its quadratic exponent makes posterior updating tractable.{{cite:gelman_bda2013}} (Ch. 2, §2.5, pp. 39–41)
normal-distribution.sampling: The Box–Muller method transforms two independent uniform draws into two independent standard normal draws; multiply either by $\sigma$ and add $\mu$, where $\mu$ is the desired mean and $\sigma$ is the positive standard deviation.{{cite:box_muller1958}} (pp. 610–611)
normal-distribution.conjugate_prior_for: $X_i\mid\mu\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with known $\sigma^2$ and prior $\mu\sim\operatorname{N}(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2)$, giving a normal posterior
normal-distribution.lead_context: Its location-scale form is used for data models and for approximations to the sampling distribution of an average.{{cite:gelman_bda2013}} (Ch. 2, §2.5, pp. 39–41)
normal-distribution.statistical_use: Normal likelihoods support estimation and intervals for a population mean when the sampling assumptions are credible. A central limit theorem may also justify an approximately normal average when the individual observations are not normal. These are different modelling claims and call for different checks.{{cite:gelman_bda2013}} (Ch. 2, §2.5, pp. 39–41) {{cite:siegrist2022_normals}} (§6.08, “The One Sample Model”)
normal-distribution.worked_example:
### One standard deviation above the mean

For $X\sim N(100,15^2)$, $P(X>115)=P(Z>1)\approx0.1587$ after standardising by the mean and standard deviation. The same tail probability applies to any normal law one standard deviation above its mean.{{cite:siegrist2022_normal_distribution}} (§5.6, “The General Normal Distribution”)

key_result.title: Affine changes preserve normality
key_result.statement: If $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ and $a\ne0$, then $aX+b\sim N(a\mu+b,a^2\sigma^2)$.{{cite:siegrist2022_normal_distribution}} (§5.6, “The General Normal Distribution”)
key_result.meaning: Changing measurement units shifts and rescales a normal law without changing its basic shape.{{cite:siegrist2022_normal_distribution}} (§5.6, “The General Normal Distribution”)

pareto-distribution.name: Pareto
pareto-distribution.description: a heavy-tailed distribution for positive quantities above a threshold
pareto-distribution.symbols: where xₘ is the minimum, α is the positive tail parameter, and x is an observed value
pareto-distribution.history:
Pareto described patterns of economic quantities in his 1909 manual of political economy. The distribution named for him represents a tail in which very large observations remain comparatively common.{{cite:pareto1909}}

Modern distribution references use its tail parameter to show exactly when the mean or variance exists. This makes the family both a model for extremes and a warning against relying on moments without checking their conditions.{{cite:forbes2011}}
pareto-distribution.sampling: Draw $U$ uniformly between zero and one and set $X=x_m(1-U)^{-1/\alpha}$, where $x_m$ is the minimum and $\alpha$ is the tail parameter.
pareto-distribution.lead_context: Its power-law tail is used to describe extreme inequality and to show when population moments may fail to exist.{{cite:forbes2011}}
pareto-distribution.statistical_use: A Pareto tail model focuses on observations above a chosen threshold, with the tail parameter governing the frequency of very large values. Moment-based summaries are inappropriate when that parameter is too small for the corresponding moment to exist.{{cite:forbes2011}}
pareto-distribution.worked_example:
### A large value above the minimum

For minimum $x_m=2$ and tail parameter $\alpha=3$, $P(X>4)=(2/4)^3=1/8$. Doubling the threshold from the minimum reduces the exceedance probability by a factor of eight.{{cite:forbes2011}}

key_result.title: Power-law survival
key_result.statement: For $X\sim\operatorname{Pareto}(x_m,\alpha)$ and $x\ge x_m$, $P(X>x)=(x_m/x)^\alpha$.{{cite:forbes2011}}
key_result.meaning: The tail probability shrinks by a fixed power when the threshold is multiplied.
key_result.proof: Integrate the density $\alpha x_m^\alpha u^{-\alpha-1}$ from $x$ to infinity: $\int_x^\infty\alpha x_m^\alpha u^{-\alpha-1}\,du=x_m^\alpha x^{-\alpha}$.{{cite:forbes2011}}

poisson-distribution.name: Poisson
poisson-distribution.description: a count distribution for events occurring at a constant average rate
poisson-distribution.symbols: where λ is the mean count and x is a nonnegative count
poisson-distribution.history:
Poisson’s 1837 treatise addressed probability questions about civil and criminal judgements and presented the count law now associated with his name.{{cite:poisson1837}}

Later probability models linked Poisson counts to events in time and space and to the rare-event limit of binomial trials. Contemporary count regression still uses the equal-mean-and-variance law as a baseline.{{cite:ross2019}}{{cite:agresti2002}}
poisson-distribution.sampling: Draw a uniform value $U$ and return the smallest count $x$ whose cumulative probability is at least $U$.
poisson-distribution.lead_context: It models counts over a fixed exposure and is the reference point for assessing count-data dispersion.{{cite:ross2019}}
poisson-distribution.statistical_use: A Poisson likelihood estimates an event rate from counts and their exposures; a regression offset can account for different exposure lengths. A variance much larger or smaller than the fitted mean indicates that its equal-mean-and-variance assumption needs checking.{{cite:agresti2002}}
poisson-distribution.worked_example:
### Two arrivals at mean three

For $X\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(3)$, $P(X=2)=e^{-3}3^2/2!\approx0.2240$. The value $3$ is the expected count for the exposure, not a maximum possible count.{{cite:ross2019}}

key_result.title: Adding independent Poisson counts
key_result.statement: If $X_1\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_1)$ and $X_2\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_2)$ are independent, then $X_1+X_2\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)$.{{cite:ross2019}}
key_result.meaning: Counts from disjoint independent exposures can be pooled by adding their expected counts.
key_result.proof: The probability-generating function of a Poisson count is $G_i(z)=\exp[\lambda_i(z-1)]$. Independence makes the generating function of the sum the product $G_1(z)G_2(z)=\exp[(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)(z-1)]$, which identifies the stated Poisson law.{{cite:ross2019}}

student-t-distribution.name: Student t
student-t-distribution.description: a symmetric heavy-tailed distribution used when a normal mean is standardised by an estimated scale
student-t-distribution.symbols: where ν is the degrees of freedom, Γ is the gamma function, and t is a value on the real line
student-t-distribution.history:
The distribution was published in 1908 under the pseudonym Student in a paper on the probable error of a mean. The problem was how to assess a sample mean when the population scale had to be estimated from the same small sample.{{cite:student1908}}

The resulting heavier-tailed reference law remains central to normal-sample intervals and tests. Its normal limit as the degrees of freedom grow explains why large-sample t and normal calculations become similar.{{cite:casella_berger2002}}
student-t-distribution.lead_context: Its heavier tails calibrate mean inference when a normal sample’s scale is estimated rather than known.{{cite:casella_berger2002}}
student-t-distribution.statistical_use: A one-sample t statistic uses an estimated standard error and has a Student t reference law under independent normal sampling. The degrees of freedom reflect how much information went into estimating that scale.{{cite:casella_berger2002}}
student-t-distribution.worked_example:
### A two-sided t tail

For $T\sim t_5$, $P(|T|>2)=2P(T>2)\approx0.1019$. Replacing this reference law by a standard normal would give a smaller tail probability and understate uncertainty in this small-degree-of-freedom example.{{cite:forbes2011}}

key_result.title: The Cauchy special case
key_result.statement: For $T\sim t_\nu$, setting $\nu=1$ gives the standard Cauchy law.{{cite:forbes2011}}
key_result.meaning: The extreme one-degree-of-freedom tail is a concrete reason to check moment conditions before using t summaries.
key_result.proof: Substitute $\nu=1$ into the Student t density. Since $\Gamma(1)=1$ and $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$, its normalising coefficient becomes $1/\pi$ and the remaining factor becomes $(1+t^2)^{-1}$. Thus $f(t)=1/[\pi(1+t^2)]$, the standard Cauchy density.{{cite:forbes2011}}

uniform-distribution.name: Uniform
uniform-distribution.description: a distribution that assigns equal density throughout an interval
uniform-distribution.symbols: where a and b are the interval endpoints and x is an observed value
uniform-distribution.sampling: Draw $U$ uniformly between zero and one and set $X=a+(b-a)U$, where $a$ and $b$ are the interval endpoints.
uniform-distribution.statistical_use: It provides the starting random draws for inverse-transform simulation and a simple model that gives equal probabilities to equal-length intervals within a bounded range. Uniform random numbers are transformed into draws from many other distributions by applying a quantile function. A uniform model for observed measurements requires a bounded range and a defensible constant-density assumption.{{cite:siegrist2022_uniform_interval}} (§5.21, Basic Theory){{cite:von_neumann1951_random_digits}} (pp. 36–38)
uniform-distribution.worked_example:
### Half the interval

For $X\sim U[2,6]$, $P(3<X<5)=(5-3)/(6-2)=1/2$. The probability is the length of the subinterval divided by the length of the full support.{{cite:siegrist2022_uniform_interval}} (§5.21, Basic Theory)

key_result.title: Mean and variance on an interval
key_result.statement: For $X\sim U[a,b]$ with $a<b$, $\mathrm E(X)=(a+b)/2$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=(b-a)^2/12$.{{cite:siegrist2022_uniform_interval}} (§5.21, Basic Theory)
key_result.meaning: The centre is the midpoint and the spread depends on interval width, not its location.
key_result.proof: Integrating $x/(b-a)$ from $a$ to $b$ gives $\mathrm E(X)=(a+b)/2$. Integrating $x^2/(b-a)$ gives $\mathrm E(X^2)=(a^2+ab+b^2)/3$. Subtracting the squared mean simplifies to $(b-a)^2/12$.{{cite:siegrist2022_uniform_interval}} (§5.21, Basic Theory)

weibull-distribution.name: Weibull
weibull-distribution.description: a positive distribution often used to model lifetimes and failure times
weibull-distribution.symbols: where k is the shape, λ is the scale, and x is a positive value
weibull-distribution.history:
Weibull presented this family in 1951 as a statistical distribution of wide applicability. Its adjustable shape made it useful when a constant failure rate was too restrictive.{{cite:weibull1951}}

Modern reliability models use its survival and hazard functions to describe ageing or early failures. The exponential model is its constant-hazard special case.{{cite:ross2019}}
weibull-distribution.sampling: Draw $U$ uniformly between zero and one and set $X=\lambda[-\log(1-U)]^{1/k}$, where $k$ is the shape and $\lambda$ the scale.
weibull-distribution.lead_context: Its shape parameter lets failure risk rise, fall or stay constant, making it a flexible lifetime model.{{cite:weibull1951}}
weibull-distribution.statistical_use: In reliability analysis, a Weibull fit separates a lifetime scale from a shape that controls the hazard over time. A shape above one describes increasing hazard, while a shape below one describes decreasing hazard; one Weibull component cannot create a bathtub-shaped hazard.{{cite:ross2019}}
weibull-distribution.worked_example:
### Survival at the scale time

For shape $k=2$ and scale $\lambda=10$ hours, $P(X>10)=e^{-(10/10)^2}=e^{-1}\approx0.3679$. At time $10$, the hazard is $(2/10)(10/10)=0.2$ per hour.{{cite:forbes2011}}
weibull-distribution.definition_note: Some sources instead use shape $\beta$ and rate $r=1/\lambda$; substituting these into the density gives the same law.{{cite:forbes2011}}

key_result.title: Survival and hazard in shape-scale form
key_result.statement: For a Weibull lifetime with shape $k$ and scale $\lambda$, $S(t)=e^{-(t/\lambda)^k}$ and $h(t)=(k/\lambda)(t/\lambda)^{k-1}$ for $t>0$.{{cite:ross2019}}
key_result.meaning: A shape above one raises the hazard with age; a shape below one lowers it.
key_result.proof: Integrating the density from $t$ to infinity gives $S(t)=e^{-(t/\lambda)^k}$. Evaluating the hazard $-d\log S(t)/dt$ gives $(k/\lambda)(t/\lambda)^{k-1}$. At $k=1$ the hazard is constant, $1/\lambda$.{{cite:ross2019}}

wishart-distribution.name: Wishart
wishart-distribution.description: a distribution for scatter matrices formed from independent normal vectors
wishart-distribution.symbols: where ν is the degrees of freedom, Σ is the scale matrix, Γₚ is the multivariate gamma function, and W is positive definite
wishart-distribution.history:
Wishart’s 1928 paper studied a generalised product-moment distribution for samples from a multivariate normal population. The random matrix arises from sums of outer products, the multivariate counterpart of sums of normal squares.{{cite:wishart1928}}

Modern multivariate analysis uses that law for covariance-matrix inference under normal sampling. Its one-dimensional case reduces to a scaled chi-squared distribution.{{cite:anderson2003_mva}}
wishart-distribution.lead_context: It generalises a chi-squared sum of squares to a random covariance or scatter matrix.{{cite:anderson2003_mva}}
wishart-distribution.statistical_use: Under multivariate-normal sampling, a scaled sample covariance matrix has a Wishart law and supports inference about covariance structure. The matrix must remain positive definite for the stated density, and the degrees of freedom govern its variability.{{cite:anderson2003_mva}}
wishart-distribution.worked_example:
### The one-dimensional case

Take $p=1$, scale $\Sigma=2$ and $
u=4$ independent normal squares. Then $W=2\chi^2_4$ has mean $
u\Sigma=8$ and variance $2
u\Sigma^2=32$. This is the scalar Wishart case.{{cite:anderson2003_mva}}
wishart-distribution.definition_note: Here $p$ is the matrix dimension and $\Gamma_p$ is the multivariate gamma function; for the normal-sample construction, integer $\nu\ge p$ is the number of independent normal vectors.{{cite:anderson2003_mva}}

key_result.title: Mean of a scatter matrix
key_result.statement: For $W\sim W_p(\Sigma,\nu)$ with the stated scale parameterisation, $\mathrm E(W)=\nu\Sigma$.{{cite:anderson2003_mva}}
key_result.meaning: The expected scatter scales with both the number of contributing vectors and their covariance.
key_result.proof:
For a symmetric test matrix $T$ near zero, the Wishart Laplace transform is $\mathrm E[e^{-\operatorname{tr}(TW)}]=|I+2\Sigma T|^{-
u/2}$, where $I$ is the identity matrix and $|\cdot|$ denotes determinant. Its directional derivative at $T=0$ in any symmetric direction $H$ is $-
u\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma H)$; the same derivative of the expectation is $-\operatorname{tr}(H\mathrm E W)$. Equality for every symmetric $H$ gives $\mathrm E W=
u\Sigma$.{{cite:anderson2003_mva}}
